---
title: "Autoencoder"
description: "A neural network trained to encode data into a representation and reconstruct the input."
term: "Autoencoder"
letter: "A"
category: "Deep Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

An autoencoder learns to compress an input into a representation and then
reconstruct the original input from that representation. Comparing the
reconstruction with the input provides a training signal.

## Technical explanation

An autoencoder contains an encoder $z = f(x)$ and a decoder
$\hat{x} = g(z)$. Training minimizes a reconstruction loss between $x$
and $\hat{x}$. Bottlenecks, noise, sparsity, or other constraints can
encourage useful representations, but the learned representation depends
on the data and objective.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Autoencoders are used for representation learning, dimensionality
reduction, denoising, and sometimes anomaly detection. Their outputs and
scores need careful validation because good reconstruction does not
necessarily correspond to semantic understanding or anomaly relevance.

## How it works

The encoder maps the input to a latent representation. The decoder maps
that representation back to the input space. The model adjusts both sets
of parameters to reduce reconstruction error, often under constraints
that prevent the trivial solution of simply copying every input detail.

## Practical example

A denoising autoencoder receives a slightly corrupted image and is trained
to reconstruct the clean version. It can learn features that help recover
common image structure from noise.

## Common misconceptions

- An autoencoder does not necessarily learn a useful or interpretable
  representation.
- Reconstruction error is not automatically a reliable anomaly score.
- A compact latent space does not guarantee that all task-relevant
  information is preserved.
